svg.title: What the days look like with the three urinary diversions: ileal conduit, orthotopic neobladder and ureterocutaneostomy, with no ranking drawn
svg.desc: Schematic showing what the days look like with each of the three urinary diversions, in three columns set out flat, the order carrying no ranking. At the top are the guideline's own two sentences: "Randomised controlled trials comparing conduit diversion with neobladder or continent cutaneous diversion have not been performed." and "Currently, it is not possible to recommend a particular type of urinary diversion." - no randomised trial has compared the three, so the guideline cannot recommend any one of them; the EAU also records that the type of diversion does not affect the cancer outcome, and the NICE wording is that people choosing radical cystectomy should be offered either a urostomy or a continent diversion unless there is a strong contraindication such as impaired cognitive function, impaired renal function or significant bowel disease. The first column is the ileal conduit, a stoma on the abdominal wall draining into a bag: the EAU calls it a mature technique with predictable results; 30-day complications 48%, mostly urinary tract infection, pyelonephritis and leak or stricture at the ureteric and ileal anastomoses; long-term stoma-related complications up to 24%; functional or morphological change in the upper tract up to 30%; and its late complications are the fewest of the three; what has to be learnt is stoma and bag care. The second column is the orthotopic neobladder, a pouch built from bowel and joined back to the urethra, emptied by abdominal pressure and relaxing the sphincter: registry data from the Netherlands, Germany and Spain put its use at roughly one to two in ten of both men and women; the EAU tabulates neobladder-related problems at 30% to 64%; prospective assessment in men shows daytime continence rising from 59% within three months of surgery to 92% at 12 to 18 months, and night-time continence from 28% to 51% at 18 to 36 months; among 56 women with a neobladder, daytime continence was 70.4% and night-time 64.8%, but difficulty emptying is particularly common in women - about two-thirds need to self-catheterise and nearly 45% cannot void spontaneously at all; what has to be learnt is timed voiding and, for some, self-catheterisation. The third column is ureterocutaneostomy, the ureters brought directly to the abdominal wall: the EAU calls it the simplest form of cutaneous diversion, with operating time, complication rate, blood loss, transfusion rate, intensive care stay and days in hospital all lower than with an ileal conduit; the price is that the ureters are narrow, so stomal stenosis and ascending urinary tract infection are more common than with a stoma built from bowel; for frail patients, or for someone with a single kidney who needs upper tract diversion, it is the first choice; what has to be learnt is stoma care and the rhythm of catheter changes. Below the three columns the figure states that they are not one ruler: one reports 30-day complications, one reports continence rates years later, and one reports the items that are lower than with another technique, so they cannot be subtracted from one another and cannot be ranked. The next panel draws out what follows from reading all three: the one least like the original bladder has the fewest late complications; the one most like the original bladder still leaves only half of patients continent at night beyond a year and a half; the simplest one is some people's first choice, not a compromise; so this is not a ranking but three different sets of days. The panel after that is the long bill, counted for all three together in one column: among 3,360 people who had a radical cystectomy for muscle-invasive bladder cancer, 29% progressed to advanced chronic kidney disease within 12 months; benign ureteric-to-bowel anastomotic stricture up to 20%; vitamin B12 low in 17% of people with a bowel diversion, which the EAU advises checking once a year; SEER data associate radical cystectomy with a 21% higher fracture risk, thought to relate to long-term metabolic acidosis and bone loss, which is an association and not a proven cause; 45% of diversion-related complications are detected in the first five years of follow-up, rising to 94% among those surviving beyond 15 years in a series of 131 patients, with 50% showing upper tract change and 38% urinary stones at 15 years; and a retrospective dataset of 1,383 patients found no significant difference between an ileal conduit and an orthotopic neobladder in the risk of a falling glomerular filtration rate, what was actually associated with the fall being age and anastomotic stricture. The next panel lists the signals that do not wait for the next appointment - there is no citable quantitative threshold for any of them, so they are written as symptoms rather than numbers: fever with one-sided loin pain; a sudden fall in the volume draining from the stoma or no urine at all for a whole day; fluid leaking continuously from the wound or around the stoma; a neobladder that will not empty together with abdominal distension - if any of them appears, contact the surgical team or go to the emergency department the same day. The same panel records that how the choice is made matters more than which one is chosen: the EAU notes that a diversion decision made by a fully informed patient is associated with less decisional regret afterwards, "independent of the method selected", and NICE requires a stoma nurse to be available to talk both before and after the operation. The last panel lists two readings the figure must not be given: "one of the three is better than the others" and "now I know which one to pick".

g.text: URINARY DIVERSION - THREE DIFFERENT DAYS,
NOT A RANKING
What the days look like
with each of the three
urinary diversions - no
ranking here, and none
in the guideline either
For someone told the bladder has to come out, the first
question is almost never the survival rate; it is "what
happens to the urine afterwards". This figure sets out
what the days look like with each diversion: what has to be
learnt, the size of the complication figures, and which
group of patients each figure comes from.
The three columns are not measured with the same ruler
- each reports different items, so no set of numbers can
be subtracted from another, and no column can be placed
ahead of another.
The licence for this section comes from the guideline itself: no
randomised trial has compared the three diversions, so the
guideline cannot recommend any one of them.
The guideline itself says they cannot be
ranked
Randomised controlled trials comparing conduit diversion
with neobladder or continent cutaneous diversion have not
been performed.
No randomised trial has compared conduit diversion with a
neobladder or a continent cutaneous diversion.
Currently, it is not possible to recommend a particular type
of urinary diversion.
At present no particular type of urinary diversion can be
recommended.
The EAU also records that the type of diversion does not affect the
cancer outcome. The NICE wording is that people choosing radical
cystectomy should be offered either a urostomy or a continent
diversion, unless there is a strong contraindication such as
impaired cognitive function, impaired renal function or significant
bowel disease.
What the days look like
Three columns set out flat; the order carries no ranking. Under each
column is a note on what its numbers actually are - the three report
different items, so there is no comparable score between them.
Ileal conduit
a stoma on the abdominal wall draining into a bag
how the guideline describes it
the EAU calls it a mature technique with predictable results
30-day complications
48%, mostly urinary tract infection, pyelonephritis, and leak or stricture at
the ureteric and ileal anastomoses
long-term stoma-related complications
up to 24%
functional or morphological change in the upper tract
up to 30%
the other side of this column
its late complications are the fewest of the three
What has to be learnt is stoma and bag care.
Orthotopic neobladder
a pouch built from bowel and joined back to the urethra, emptied by
abdominal pressure and relaxing the sphincter
how many people have one
registry data from the Netherlands, Germany and Spain put it at roughly one
to two in ten of both men and women
neobladder-related problems
the EAU tabulates a rate of 30% to 64%
prospective assessment in men
daytime continence rises from 59% within three months of surgery to 92% at
12 to 18 months; night-time from 28% to 51% at 18 to 36 months
56 women with a neobladder
daytime continence 70.4%, night-time 64.8%
difficulty emptying, in women
about two-thirds need to self-catheterise and nearly 45% cannot void
spontaneously at all
What has to be learnt is timed voiding and, for some,
self-catheterisation.
Ureterocutaneostomy
the ureters brought directly to the abdominal wall
how the guideline describes it
the EAU calls it the simplest form of cutaneous diversion
items lower than with an ileal conduit
operating time, complication rate, blood loss, transfusion rate, intensive
care stay and days in hospital
the price
the ureters are narrow, so stomal stenosis and ascending urinary tract
infection are more common than with a stoma built from bowel
whose first choice it is
for frail patients, or for someone with a single kidney who needs upper
tract diversion, it is the first choice
What has to be learnt is stoma care, and the rhythm of catheter
changes.
The three columns are not one ruler: one reports 30-day complications,
one reports continence rates years later, and one reports the items that
are lower than with another technique. They cannot be subtracted from
one another, and they cannot be ranked.
Read all three and one thing follows
The one least like the original bladder has the fewest late
complications.
The one most like the original bladder still leaves only half of
patients continent at night beyond a year and a half.
The simplest one is some people's first choice, not a
compromise.
So this is not a ranking. It is three different sets of
days.
The long bill: this panel counts for all three
together, in one column
kidney function
among 3,360 people who had a radical cystectomy for muscle-invasive
bladder cancer, 29% progressed to advanced chronic kidney disease
within 12 months
anastomotic stricture
benign ureteric-to-bowel anastomotic stricture up to 20%
vitamin B12
low in 17% of people with a bowel diversion; the EAU advises checking it
once a year
bone
SEER data associate radical cystectomy with a 21% higher fracture risk,
thought to relate to long-term metabolic acidosis and bone loss - that is an
association, not a proven cause
the timeline
45% of diversion-related complications are detected in the first five years
of follow-up; in a series of 131 patients it rose to 94% among those
surviving beyond 15 years, with 50% showing upper tract change and 38%
urinary stones at 15 years
And a retrospective dataset of 1,383 patients found no
significant difference between an ileal conduit and an
orthotopic neobladder in the risk of a falling glomerular
filtration rate; what was actually associated with the fall was
age and anastomotic stricture.
These do not wait for the next appointment
There is no citable quantitative threshold for any of these, so what is
written here is symptoms, not numbers. If any of them appears,
contact your surgical team or go to the emergency department the
same day.
fever with one-sided loin pain (this is often what
pyelonephritis or a stricture at the anastomosis looks like)
a sudden fall in the volume draining from the stoma, or no
urine at all for a whole day
fluid leaking continuously from the wound or around the
stoma (this is what an anastomotic leak looks like)
a neobladder that will not empty, together with abdominal
distension
How the choice is made matters more than which one is chosen.
The EAU records that a diversion decision made by a fully
informed patient is associated with less decisional regret
afterwards, and that this is "independent of the method selected" -
it has nothing to do with which one was chosen in the end. NICE
requires a stoma nurse to be available to talk both before and after
the operation.
Two readings this figure must not be given
"one of the three is better than the others"
The guideline itself says no randomised trial has compared
them and that none can be recommended over another; and the
type of diversion does not affect the cancer outcome.
"now I know which one to pick"
Which one suits you depends on kidney function, the state of the
bowel, hand dexterity, cognitive function and how your own
days are spent; it is worked out with your surgical team and
stoma nurse, not picked off a table.
Schematic, redrawn from the EAU guidelines on muscle-invasive and
metastatic bladder cancer (2026 edition) and NICE NG2; not reproduced
from their figures. The cohorts, designs and endpoints of the underlying
studies differ, so the data points must not be compared directly.
